title: Vibrations and Waves
topics: Wave motion and the wave equation

items.q: A mass of 0.2 kg hangs on a spring of constant 80 N/m and oscillates. Take pi as 3.142 and calculate the period in s.
items.s: The period is twice pi times the square root of mass divided by spring constant = 0.3142 s.

items.q: A spring of constant 200 N/m is stretched by 0.2 m. Calculate the stored energy in J.
items.s: Stored energy is half the spring constant times the extension squared = 0.5 x 200 x 0.2 x 0.2 = 4 J.

items.q: A wave of frequency 50 Hz travels with a wavelength of 0.5 m. Calculate its speed in m/s.
items.s: Wave speed is frequency times wavelength = 50 x 0.5 = 25 m/s.
items.t: Wave motion and the wave equation

items.q: A sound wave travels at 320 m/s with a wavelength of 3 m. Calculate its frequency in Hz.
items.s: Frequency is speed divided by wavelength = 320 / 3 = 106.7 Hz.
items.t: Wave motion and the wave equation

items.q: A wave has a frequency of 20 Hz. Calculate its period in ms.
items.s: The period is the reciprocal of the frequency, 1/20 = 0.05 thousandths of a second, or 50 ms.
items.t: Wave motion and the wave equation

items.q: Two waves arriving at a point produce displacements of 3 units and 3 units in the same direction. Calculate the resultant displacement in the same units.
items.s: By superposition the displacements add directly when they act in the same direction, giving 3 + 3 = 6 units.

items.q: Two waves arriving at a point produce displacements of 10 units and 3 units in opposite directions. Calculate the magnitude of the resultant displacement in the same units.
items.s: Opposite displacements partly cancel, so the resultant magnitude is 10 - 3 = 7 units.

items.q: A pipe closed at one end has a length of 0.3 m. Taking the speed of sound as 350 m/s, calculate its fundamental frequency in Hz.
items.s: A pipe stopped at one end has its lowest resonance at a quarter of a wavelength, so the frequency is 350 / (4 x 0.3) = 291.7 Hz.

items.q: A pipe open at both ends has a length of 0.1 m. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m/s, calculate its fundamental frequency in Hz.
items.s: A pipe open at both ends has its lowest resonance at half a wavelength, so the frequency is 340 / (2 x 0.1) = 1700 Hz.

items.q: An aircraft travels at 680 m/s in air where the speed of sound is 340 m/s. Calculate its Mach number.
items.s: The Mach number is the speed of the body divided by the speed of sound = 680 / 340 = 2.

items.q: Two waves of frequencies 512 Hz and 522 Hz travel together. Calculate the beat frequency heard in Hz.
items.s: The beat frequency is the difference of the two frequencies = 10 Hz.

items.q: A body in simple harmonic motion has a maximum speed of 4 m/s at a rate of 6 rad/s. Calculate its amplitude in m.
items.s: Maximum speed is amplitude times angular frequency, so the amplitude is 4 / 6 = 0.6667 m.

items.q: A body oscillates with simple harmonic motion of amplitude 0.25 m at an angular frequency of 5 rad/s. Calculate its maximum acceleration in m/s squared.
items.s: Maximum acceleration is amplitude times the square of the angular frequency = 0.25 x 5 x 5 = 6.25 m/s squared.

items.q: An oscillator of amplitude 0.5 m and angular frequency 10 rad/s starts from its greatest displacement. Calculate its displacement 0.3 s after release, in m.
items.s: The displacement is amplitude times the cosine of the angular frequency times the time = 0.5 x cos(3) = -0.495 m.

items.q: A simple pendulum has an effective length of 0.5 m. Take g as 9.8 m/s squared and pi as 3.142, and calculate its period in s.
items.s: The period is twice pi times the square root of the length divided by g = 2 x 3.142 x sqrt(0.5/9.8) = 1.42 s.

items.q: A simple pendulum has a period of 3 s. Take g as 9.8 m/s squared and pi as 3.142, and calculate its effective length in m.
items.s: The length is g times the square of the period divided by four pi squared = 9.8 x 3 x 3 / 39.48 = 2.23 m.

items.q: A mass of 3 kg hung on a spring extends it by 0.2 m. Take g as 9.8 m/s squared and calculate the spring constant in N/m.
items.s: At rest the weight balances the restoring pull, so the constant is 3 x 9.8 / 0.2 = 147 N/m.

items.q: A body of moment of inertia 0.05 kg m squared is suspended from a wire of torsional stiffness 2.5 N m per radian. Take pi as 3.142 and calculate the period of twist in s.
items.s: The period is twice pi times the square root of the moment of inertia divided by the torsional stiffness = 0.8887 s.

items.q: A mass of 0.1 kg oscillates with simple harmonic motion of amplitude 0.02 m at angular frequency 5 rad/s. Calculate the total energy of the oscillation in J.
items.s: Total energy is half the mass times the square of the angular frequency times the amplitude squared = 0.0005 J.

items.q: An oscillator transfers 0.5 J of energy in 1 s. Calculate the average rate at which energy is transferred in W.
items.s: The average rate is the energy divided by the time = 0.5 / 1 = 0.5 W.

items.q: An oscillator has a total energy of 0.5 J. Calculate its stored energy when its displacement is 0.75 of the amplitude.
items.s: Stored energy varies as the square of the displacement, so it is 0.5 x (0.75 x 0.75) = 0.2812 J.

items.q: Two tuning forks of frequencies 480 Hz and 484 Hz sound together. Calculate the number of beats heard per second.
items.s: The number of beats per second equals the difference of the two frequencies = 4 Hz.

items.q: A lightly damped oscillator of initial amplitude 1 m decays with a damping coefficient of 1.5 per s. Calculate its amplitude after 2 s, in m.
items.s: The amplitude falls as the initial value times the exponential of minus the damping coefficient times the time = 0.0498 m.

items.q: The amplitude of a damped oscillator falls from 10 units to a steady value after 4 complete oscillations at the same fractional loss each time. Taking the amplitude after those oscillations as 10 units divided by the number of oscillations, calculate the amplitude after one oscillation in the same units.
items.s: Losing the same fraction each cycle divides the starting amplitude by the number of oscillations, giving 10 = 2.5 units.

items.q: A driven electrical oscillator has an inductance of 0.2 H and a capacitance of 50 microfarad. Taking pi as 3.142, calculate the frequency at which resonance occurs in Hz.
items.s: Resonance occurs at one divided by twice pi times the square root of inductance times capacitance = 50.32 Hz.

items.q: A wave of frequency 50 Hz travels at 300 m/s. Calculate its wavelength in m.
items.s: Wavelength is speed divided by frequency = 300 / 50 = 6 m.
items.t: Wave motion and the wave equation

items.q: A wave has a wavelength of 0.4 m. Calculate its wave number in per m.
items.s: The wave number is the reciprocal of the wavelength = 1/0.4 = 2.5 per m.
items.t: Wave motion and the wave equation

items.q: A standing wave has a wavelength of 0.8 m. Calculate the distance between two neighbouring nodes in m.
items.s: Neighbouring nodes are half a wavelength apart, so the distance is 0.8 / 2 = 0.4 m.

items.q: The fundamental frequency of a stretched string is 80 Hz. Calculate the frequency of its 6 harmonic in Hz.
items.s: The harmonics are whole number multiples of the fundamental, so the 6 harmonic is 80 x 6 = 480 Hz.

items.q: A string of length 1.2 m and mass per unit length 0.025 kg/m is stretched with a tension of 40 N. Calculate its fundamental frequency in Hz.
items.s: The wave speed is the square root of tension over mass per unit length, and the fundamental is that speed divided by twice the length = 16.67 Hz.

items.q: A string of length 0.5 m vibrates in 5 loops. Calculate the wavelength of the standing wave in m.
items.s: With 5 loops the wavelength is twice the length divided by the number of loops = 0.2 m.

items.q: A pipe closed at one end has a fundamental frequency of 150 Hz. Calculate the frequency of its 9 harmonic in Hz.
items.s: A stopped pipe supports only odd multiples of the fundamental, so the 9 harmonic is 150 x 9 = 1350 Hz.

items.q: A resonance tube closed at one end resounds first at a length of 0.18 m. Neglecting the end correction, calculate the next resonant length in m.
items.s: Successive resonances in a stopped pipe are separated by half a wavelength, and the sequence goes from a quarter to three quarters of a wavelength, so the next length is 3 x 0.18 = 0.54 m.

items.q: A stopped resonance tube resounds at lengths of 0.1 m and 0.3 m. Calculate the end correction in m.
items.s: The end correction is half of (second length - three times the first length) = (0.3 - 3 x 0.1)/2 = -0 m.

items.q: A source emits 0.01 W of sound energy that falls normally on a surface of area 0.5 m squared. Calculate the intensity at the surface in W per m squared.
items.s: Intensity is the energy crossing unit area per second = 0.01 / 0.5 = 0.02 W per m squared.

items.q: A sound has an intensity 10000 times the threshold of hearing taken as 10^-12 W per m squared. Calculate its level in decibel.
items.s: The level is ten times the logarithm to base ten of the ratio to the threshold, giving 30 decibel.

items.q: A source emitting 500 Hz approaches a stationary listener at 30 m/s. Taking the speed of sound as 360 m/s, calculate the frequency heard in Hz.
items.s: An approaching source crowds its waves, so the observed frequency is 500 x 360 / (360 - 30) = 545.5 Hz.

items.q: A source emitting 500 Hz recedes from a stationary listener at 20 m/s. Taking the speed of sound as 360 m/s, calculate the frequency heard in Hz.
items.s: A receding source stretches its waves, so the observed frequency is 500 x 360 / (360 + 20) = 473.7 Hz.

items.q: A listener moves towards a stationary source of frequency 800 Hz at 30 m/s. Taking the speed of sound as 320 m/s, calculate the frequency heard in Hz.
items.s: A listener moving into the waves meets more of them each second, so the observed frequency is 800 x (320 + 30) / 320 = 875 Hz.

items.q: A source of frequency 800 Hz moves away from an observer at 10 m/s. Taking the speed of sound as 330 m/s, calculate the wavelength heard in m.
items.s: The waves are stretched, so the observed wavelength is (330 + 10) / 800 = 0.425 m.

items.q: Two waves of frequencies 400 Hz and 402 Hz are superposed. Calculate the time from one loudness maximum to the next, in s.
items.s: Loudness maxima recur once per beat, and the beat frequency is 2 Hz, so the time between maxima is 1/2 = 0.5 s.

items.q: Two waves of wavelength 0.5 m reach a point with a path difference of 0.25 of a wavelength. Taking pi as 3.142, calculate the phase difference in radian.
items.s: A path difference of 0.25 of a wavelength corresponds to the same fraction of a full cycle of 2 pi, giving 1.57 radian.

items.q: Two waves of wavelength 1.5 m differ in phase by 1 of a cycle. Calculate the path difference between them in m.
items.s: The path difference is the same fraction of a wavelength = 1 x 1.5 = 1.5 m.

items.q: A source has a coherence time of 2e-09 s. Taking the speed of light as 3.0 x 10^8 m/s, calculate its coherence length in m.
items.s: Coherence length is the speed of light times the coherence time = 3.0 x 10^8 x 2e-09 = 0.6 m.

items.q: Two identical coupled oscillators share a total energy of 0.5 J. Calculate the energy in one of them when 0.5 of the total has passed across, in J.
items.s: The energy that has passed across is 0.5 x 0.5 = 0.25 J.

items.q: Two coupled pendulums of natural frequencies 2 Hz and 5 Hz swing together in step. Calculate the frequency of this common mode in Hz.
items.s: In the in step mode the two swing as one system at the average of their separate frequencies = (2 + 5)/2 = 3.5 Hz.

items.q: Two coupled oscillators of natural frequencies 5 Hz and 8 Hz exchange energy. Calculate the frequency of the slow transfer back and forth in Hz.
items.s: Energy passes across and back once per beat, so the transfer frequency is the difference of the two natural frequencies = 3 Hz.

items.q: A pendulum of small swing period 1.5 s is swung through an amplitude of 10 degrees. Using the correction that adds the square of the amplitude in degrees divided by 16000, calculate its period in s.
items.s: The period lengthens slightly with amplitude, giving 1.5 x (1 + 100/16000) = 1.51 s.

items.q: An oscillator completes 5 cycles every second. Calculate its period in s.
items.s: The period is the reciprocal of the number of cycles per second = 1/5 = 0.2 s.

items.q: A mass of 0.25 kg hangs on a spring of constant 80 N/m and oscillates. Take pi as 3.142 and calculate the period in s.
items.s: The period is twice pi times the square root of mass divided by spring constant = 0.3513 s.

items.q: A spring of constant 100 N/m is stretched by 0.2 m. Calculate the stored energy in J.
items.s: Stored energy is half the spring constant times the extension squared = 0.5 x 100 x 0.2 x 0.2 = 2 J.

items.q: A wave of frequency 500 Hz travels with a wavelength of 2 m. Calculate its speed in m/s.
items.s: Wave speed is frequency times wavelength = 500 x 2 = 1000 m/s.
items.t: Wave motion and the wave equation

items.q: A sound wave travels at 320 m/s with a wavelength of 2.5 m. Calculate its frequency in Hz.
items.s: Frequency is speed divided by wavelength = 320 / 2.5 = 128 Hz.
items.t: Wave motion and the wave equation

items.q: Two waves arriving at a point produce displacements of 5 units and 3 units in the same direction. Calculate the resultant displacement in the same units.
items.s: By superposition the displacements add directly when they act in the same direction, giving 5 + 3 = 8 units.

items.q: Two waves arriving at a point produce displacements of 5 units and 3 units in opposite directions. Calculate the magnitude of the resultant displacement in the same units.
items.s: Opposite displacements partly cancel, so the resultant magnitude is 5 - 3 = 2 units.

items.q: A pipe closed at one end has a length of 0.15 m. Taking the speed of sound as 320 m/s, calculate its fundamental frequency in Hz.
items.s: A pipe stopped at one end has its lowest resonance at a quarter of a wavelength, so the frequency is 320 / (4 x 0.15) = 533.3 Hz.

items.q: A pipe open at both ends has a length of 0.1 m. Taking the speed of sound as 320 m/s, calculate its fundamental frequency in Hz.
items.s: A pipe open at both ends has its lowest resonance at half a wavelength, so the frequency is 320 / (2 x 0.1) = 1600 Hz.

items.q: An aircraft travels at 170 m/s in air where the speed of sound is 330 m/s. Calculate its Mach number.
items.s: The Mach number is the speed of the body divided by the speed of sound = 170 / 330 = 0.5152.

items.q: Two waves of frequencies 440 Hz and 450 Hz travel together. Calculate the beat frequency heard in Hz.
items.s: The beat frequency is the difference of the two frequencies = 10 Hz.

items.q: A body in simple harmonic motion has a maximum speed of 2 m/s at a rate of 6 rad/s. Calculate its amplitude in m.
items.s: Maximum speed is amplitude times angular frequency, so the amplitude is 2 / 6 = 0.3333 m.

items.q: Which statement correctly defines effective length?
o: the distance from the point of suspension to the centre of the bob of a hanging oscillator
the position at which a swung body momentarily comes to rest and reverses
a small heavy bob hanging on a light thread from a fixed point
a tube with both ends unstopped, supporting every whole multiple of the lowest frequency
items.s: effective length: the distance from the point of suspension to the centre of the bob of a hanging oscillator. The other options describe open pipe, simple pendulum, turning point.

items.q: Which statement correctly defines transverse wave?
o: how clearly the bright and dark bands of an interference pattern stand out from each other
decay in which the oscillator completes several noticeable swings before settling
a moving emitter whose waves are stretched so the observed rate falls
a travelling disturbance whose vibration is at right angles to the direction of travel
items.s: transverse wave: a travelling disturbance whose vibration is at right angles to the direction of travel. The other options describe fringe visibility, light damping, receding source.
items.t: Wave motion and the wave equation

items.q: non linear response may be defined as
o: the lengthening of the period of a hanging oscillator that occurs as its swing grows
two or more oscillating bodies linked so that energy passes repeatedly between them
behaviour in which the size of the restoring influence grows faster or slower than the displacement
the slow rise and fall of loudness heard when two nearly equal frequencies sound together
items.s: non linear response: behaviour in which the size of the restoring influence grows faster or slower than the displacement. The other options describe large amplitude effect, beats, coupled oscillators.

items.q: Which of the following best describes damping coefficient?
o: a travelling disturbance whose vibration is at right angles to the direction of travel
the constant that fixes the rate at which the amplitude of a decaying oscillation shrinks
the number of complete cycles completed in one second
a pipe used with a tuning source to find the lengths that give the loudest response
items.s: damping coefficient: the constant that fixes the rate at which the amplitude of a decaying oscillation shrinks. The other options describe resonance tube, transverse wave, frequency.

items.q: Which term is described by “the pull or push that always acts to bring an oscillator back towards its central position”?
o: angular frequency
simple harmonic motion
period
restoring influence
items.s: restoring influence is the pull or push that always acts to bring an oscillator back towards its central position.

items.q: Which of the following best describes isochronous oscillation?
o: the condition of two waves whose crests arrive at opposite instants
the continual exchange between moving and stored parts while their sum stays fixed
a repeating motion whose cycle time does not depend on the size of the swing
the number of complete cycles completed in one second
items.s: isochronous oscillation: a repeating motion whose cycle time does not depend on the size of the swing. The other options describe out of phase, energy trade off, frequency.

items.q: Which of the following best describes shock wavefront?
o: a listener whose own movement changes the rate at which waves reach the ear
the piled up disturbance formed when an emitter outruns the waves it produces
the distance from the point of suspension to the centre of the bob of a hanging oscillator
the slow rise and fall of loudness heard when two nearly equal frequencies sound together
items.s: shock wavefront: the piled up disturbance formed when an emitter outruns the waves it produces. The other options describe observer in motion, beats, effective length.

items.q: frequency may be defined as
o: the portion of a standing pattern between two neighbouring fixed points
the fraction of a cycle by which one wave leads or lags another
the number of complete cycles completed in one second
the acoustic energy crossing unit area per second at a point
items.s: frequency: the number of complete cycles completed in one second. The other options describe intensity of sound, loop, phase difference.

items.q: Which of the following best describes mass spring system?
o: a block attached to an elastic coil that oscillates when displaced from rest
the rate at which a system oscillates freely when left to itself
the slow rise and fall of loudness heard when two nearly equal frequencies sound together
the motion of an oscillator driven by a repeated external push
items.s: mass spring system: a block attached to an elastic coil that oscillates when displaced from rest. The other options describe forced oscillation, natural frequency, beats.

items.q: Which term is described by “the fraction of a cycle by which one wave leads or lags another”?
o: beats
phase difference
in phase
out of phase
items.s: phase difference is the fraction of a cycle by which one wave leads or lags another.

items.q: All of the following belong to The pendulum and spring oscillators EXCEPT
o: simple pendulum
interference pattern
spring constant
isochronous oscillation
items.s: Every other option belongs to The pendulum and spring oscillators. “interference pattern” belongs to Wave optics and beats, not The pendulum and spring oscillators.

items.q: The statement “a frequency above the lowest at which a system can stand in a stable pattern” describes which of the following?
o: fundamental
overtone
node
antinode
items.s: overtone is a frequency above the lowest at which a system can stand in a stable pattern.

items.q: The statement “a region of a sound wave where the particles are spread apart” describes which of the following?
o: rarefaction
end correction
open pipe
resonance tube
items.s: rarefaction is a region of a sound wave where the particles are spread apart.

items.q: Which of the following best describes anharmonic oscillator?
o: the rate at which a crest advances through the medium
the resting place of an oscillator where no restoring pull acts
a vibrating body whose restoring influence is not proportional to the displacement
the piled up disturbance formed when an emitter outruns the waves it produces
items.s: anharmonic oscillator: a vibrating body whose restoring influence is not proportional to the displacement. The other options describe equilibrium position, wave speed, shock wavefront.

items.q: Which term is described by “the large response that occurs when the driving frequency matches a natural frequency”?
o: damping coefficient
light damping
resonance
forced oscillation
items.s: resonance is the large response that occurs when the driving frequency matches a natural frequency.

items.q: The statement “the progressive loss of amplitude of an oscillation because energy is steadily removed” describes which of the following?
o: damping
critical damping
heavy damping
damping coefficient
items.s: damping is the progressive loss of amplitude of an oscillation because energy is steadily removed.

items.q: Which of the following best describes torsional oscillator?
o: a body hung from a wire that twists and untwists about its own axis
a region of a sound wave where the particles are spread apart
the motion of an oscillator driven by a repeated external push
a frequency that is a whole number multiple of the lowest one
items.s: torsional oscillator: a body hung from a wire that twists and untwists about its own axis. The other options describe harmonic, rarefaction, forced oscillation.

items.q: Which statement correctly defines torsional oscillator?
o: the acoustic energy crossing unit area per second at a point
a body hung from a wire that twists and untwists about its own axis
how many complete cycles are contained in a unit of length
the small swing simplification that treats the restoring influence of a hanging bob as proportional to its displacement
items.s: torsional oscillator: a body hung from a wire that twists and untwists about its own axis. The other options describe wave number, intensity of sound, pendulum approximation.

items.q: turning point may be defined as
o: the large response that occurs when the driving frequency matches a natural frequency
the ratio of the speed of a body to the speed of sound in the same medium
energy loss so large that a displaced body creeps back to rest without ever overshooting
the position at which a swung body momentarily comes to rest and reverses
items.s: turning point: the position at which a swung body momentarily comes to rest and reverses. The other options describe mach number, resonance, heavy damping.

items.q: Which statement correctly defines closed pipe?
o: how many complete cycles are contained in a unit of length
the distance from the point of suspension to the centre of the bob of a hanging oscillator
a tube stopped at one end, supporting only odd multiples of the lowest frequency
a tube with both ends unstopped, supporting every whole multiple of the lowest frequency
items.s: closed pipe: a tube stopped at one end, supporting only odd multiples of the lowest frequency. The other options describe effective length, wave number, open pipe.

items.q: Which statement correctly defines restoring influence?
o: the pull or push that always acts to bring an oscillator back towards its central position
the position at which a swung body momentarily comes to rest and reverses
the constant that fixes the rate at which the amplitude of a decaying oscillation shrinks
a region of a sound wave where the particles are crowded together
items.s: restoring influence: the pull or push that always acts to bring an oscillator back towards its central position. The other options describe damping coefficient, compression, turning point.

items.q: standing wave may be defined as
o: the continual exchange between moving and stored parts while their sum stays fixed
a fixed pattern of still points and swinging points produced by two equal trains travelling in opposite directions
the greatest displacement of an oscillator from its central position
the portion of a standing pattern between two neighbouring fixed points
items.s: standing wave: a fixed pattern of still points and swinging points produced by two equal trains travelling in opposite directions. The other options describe energy trade off, amplitude, loop.

items.q: superposition principle may be defined as
o: the rule that at any point the resultant displacement is the sum of the displacements of the separate waves
behaviour in which the size of the restoring influence grows faster or slower than the displacement
how many complete cycles are contained in a unit of length
the distance from the point of suspension to the centre of the bob of a hanging oscillator
items.s: superposition principle: the rule that at any point the resultant displacement is the sum of the displacements of the separate waves. The other options describe effective length, wave number, non linear response.

items.q: Which statement correctly defines fundamental?
o: a tube with both ends unstopped, supporting every whole multiple of the lowest frequency
the rate at which a crest advances through the medium
the lowest frequency at which a system can stand in a stable pattern
how many complete cycles are contained in a unit of length
items.s: fundamental: the lowest frequency at which a system can stand in a stable pattern. The other options describe open pipe, wave speed, wave number.

items.q: The statement “a frequency that is a whole number multiple of the lowest one” describes which of the following?
o: antinode
standing wave
harmonic
fundamental
items.s: harmonic is a frequency that is a whole number multiple of the lowest one.

items.q: Choose the option that correctly defines out of phase.
o: the condition of two waves whose crests arrive at opposite instants
the condition of two waves whose crests arrive at the same instant
the rate at which the moving and stored parts of the motion trade places
a region of a sound wave where the particles are crowded together
items.s: out of phase: the condition of two waves whose crests arrive at opposite instants. The other options describe compression, in phase, power flow in a swing.

items.q: Which term is described by “a tube with both ends unstopped, supporting every whole multiple of the lowest frequency”?
o: compression
open pipe
end correction
intensity of sound
items.s: open pipe is a tube with both ends unstopped, supporting every whole multiple of the lowest frequency.

items.q: transverse wave may be defined as
o: a pattern in which every part of a linked system oscillates at one common rate
the stage a cycle has reached at a given instant, stated as an angle
how many complete cycles are contained in a unit of length
a travelling disturbance whose vibration is at right angles to the direction of travel
items.s: transverse wave: a travelling disturbance whose vibration is at right angles to the direction of travel. The other options describe wave number, normal mode, phase.
items.t: Wave motion and the wave equation

items.q: Choose the option that correctly defines overtone.
o: how clearly the bright and dark bands of an interference pattern stand out from each other
a frequency that is a whole number multiple of the lowest one
the force needed per unit extension of an elastic coil
a frequency above the lowest at which a system can stand in a stable pattern
items.s: overtone: a frequency above the lowest at which a system can stand in a stable pattern. The other options describe fringe visibility, harmonic, spring constant.

items.q: The statement “the time taken for one complete cycle of an oscillation” describes which of the following?
o: period
restoring influence
displacement
simple harmonic motion
items.s: period is the time taken for one complete cycle of an oscillation.

items.q: Which term is described by “a disturbance that transfers energy through space without transporting the material of the medium”?
o: plane wave
wave speed
longitudinal wave
wave
items.s: wave is a disturbance that transfers energy through space without transporting the material of the medium.
items.t: Wave motion and the wave equation

items.q: beat frequency may be defined as
o: the number of loudness maxima heard per second from two nearly equal frequencies
a tube with both ends unstopped, supporting every whole multiple of the lowest frequency
a region of a sound wave where the particles are crowded together
the portion of a standing pattern between two neighbouring fixed points
items.s: beat frequency: the number of loudness maxima heard per second from two nearly equal frequencies. The other options describe compression, loop, open pipe.

items.q: Choose the option that correctly defines wave speed.
o: a tube stopped at one end, supporting only odd multiples of the lowest frequency
the progressive loss of amplitude of an oscillation because energy is steadily removed
the rate at which a crest advances through the medium
a block attached to an elastic coil that oscillates when displaced from rest
items.s: wave speed: the rate at which a crest advances through the medium. The other options describe damping, mass spring system, closed pipe.
items.t: Wave motion and the wave equation

items.q: Which of the following best describes standing wave?
o: the number of complete cycles completed in one second
a block attached to an elastic coil that oscillates when displaced from rest
how many complete cycles are contained in a unit of length
a fixed pattern of still points and swinging points produced by two equal trains travelling in opposite directions
items.s: standing wave: a fixed pattern of still points and swinging points produced by two equal trains travelling in opposite directions. The other options describe wave number, mass spring system, frequency.

items.q: Which of the following best describes superposition principle?
o: the lengthening of the period of a hanging oscillator that occurs as its swing grows
the distance between two successive points in step on a wave
the condition of two waves whose crests arrive at opposite instants
the rule that at any point the resultant displacement is the sum of the displacements of the separate waves
items.s: superposition principle: the rule that at any point the resultant displacement is the sum of the displacements of the separate waves. The other options describe large amplitude effect, out of phase, wavelength.

items.q: energy trade off may be defined as
o: an oscillation in which the restoring influence is proportional to the displacement and directed towards the centre
the lengthening of the period of a hanging oscillator that occurs as its swing grows
the distance between two successive points in step on a wave
the continual exchange between moving and stored parts while their sum stays fixed
items.s: energy trade off: the continual exchange between moving and stored parts while their sum stays fixed. The other options describe large amplitude effect, simple harmonic motion, wavelength.

items.q: Which statement correctly defines pendulum approximation?
o: the rate at which a system oscillates freely when left to itself
a pattern in which every part of a linked system oscillates at one common rate
the small swing simplification that treats the restoring influence of a hanging bob as proportional to its displacement
two or more oscillating bodies linked so that energy passes repeatedly between them
items.s: pendulum approximation: the small swing simplification that treats the restoring influence of a hanging bob as proportional to its displacement. The other options describe natural frequency, coupled oscillators, normal mode.

items.q: Which term is described by “the lengthening of the period of a hanging oscillator that occurs as its swing grows”?
o: non linear response
large amplitude effect
normal mode
pendulum approximation
items.s: large amplitude effect is the lengthening of the period of a hanging oscillator that occurs as its swing grows.

items.q: Which term is described by “the shock disturbance produced when a source travels faster than the waves it emits”?
o: sonic boom
shock wavefront

items.q: A simple pendulum has an effective length of 2.5 m. Take g as 9.8 m/s squared and pi as 3.142, and calculate its period in s.

items.q: A mass of 3 kg hung on a spring extends it by 0.05 m. Take g as 9.8 m/s squared and calculate the spring constant in N/m.

items.q: A mass of 0.1 kg oscillates with simple harmonic motion of amplitude 0.1 m at angular frequency 15 rad/s. Calculate the total energy of the oscillation in J.
items.s: Total energy is half the mass times the square of the angular frequency times the amplitude squared = 0.1125 J.

items.q: An oscillator transfers 0.5 J of energy in 2.5 s. Calculate the average rate at which energy is transferred in W.
items.s: The average rate is the energy divided by the time = 0.5 / 2.5 = 0.2 W.

items.q: Two tuning forks of frequencies 500 Hz and 503 Hz sound together. Calculate the number of beats heard per second.
items.s: The number of beats per second equals the difference of the two frequencies = 3 Hz.

items.q: A wave of frequency 400 Hz travels at 320 m/s. Calculate its wavelength in m.
items.s: Wavelength is speed divided by frequency = 320 / 400 = 0.8 m.
items.t: Wave motion and the wave equation

items.q: A wave has a wavelength of 0.25 m. Calculate its wave number in per m.
items.s: The wave number is the reciprocal of the wavelength = 1/0.25 = 4 per m.
items.t: Wave motion and the wave equation

items.q: A standing wave has a wavelength of 0.2 m. Calculate the distance between two neighbouring nodes in m.
items.s: Neighbouring nodes are half a wavelength apart, so the distance is 0.2 / 2 = 0.1 m.

items.q: A pipe closed at one end has a fundamental frequency of 120 Hz. Calculate the frequency of its 9 harmonic in Hz.
items.s: A stopped pipe supports only odd multiples of the fundamental, so the 9 harmonic is 120 x 9 = 1080 Hz.

items.q: A source emits 0.1 W of sound energy that falls normally on a surface of area 5 m squared. Calculate the intensity at the surface in W per m squared.
items.s: Intensity is the energy crossing unit area per second = 0.1 / 5 = 0.02 W per m squared.

items.q: A source emitting 600 Hz approaches a stationary listener at 40 m/s. Taking the speed of sound as 320 m/s, calculate the frequency heard in Hz.
items.s: An approaching source crowds its waves, so the observed frequency is 600 x 320 / (320 - 40) = 685.7 Hz.

items.q: A source emitting 250 Hz recedes from a stationary listener at 10 m/s. Taking the speed of sound as 320 m/s, calculate the frequency heard in Hz.
items.s: A receding source stretches its waves, so the observed frequency is 250 x 320 / (320 + 10) = 242.4 Hz.

items.q: Two waves of frequencies 400 Hz and 405 Hz are superposed. Calculate the time from one loudness maximum to the next, in s.
items.s: Loudness maxima recur once per beat, and the beat frequency is 5 Hz, so the time between maxima is 1/5 = 0.2 s.

items.q: Two identical coupled oscillators share a total energy of 2 J. Calculate the energy in one of them when 0.25 of the total has passed across, in J.
items.s: The energy that has passed across is 2 x 0.25 = 0.5 J.

items.q: An oscillator completes 4 cycles every second. Calculate its period in s.
items.s: The period is the reciprocal of the number of cycles per second = 1/4 = 0.25 s.

items.q: A body oscillates with simple harmonic motion of amplitude 0.4 m at an angular frequency of 5 rad/s. Calculate its maximum acceleration in m/s squared.
items.s: Maximum acceleration is amplitude times the square of the angular frequency = 0.4 x 5 x 5 = 10 m/s squared.

items.q: An oscillator of amplitude 0.5 m and angular frequency 10 rad/s starts from its greatest displacement. Calculate its displacement 0.2 s after release, in m.
items.s: The displacement is amplitude times the cosine of the angular frequency times the time = 0.5 x cos(2) = -0.2081 m.

items.q: A mass of 0.4 kg hangs on a spring of constant 200 N/m and oscillates. Take pi as 3.142 and calculate the period in s.
items.s: The period is twice pi times the square root of mass divided by spring constant = 0.281 s.

items.q: A simple pendulum has a period of 1.5 s. Take g as 9.8 m/s squared and pi as 3.142, and calculate its effective length in m.
items.s: The length is g times the square of the period divided by four pi squared = 9.8 x 1.5 x 1.5 / 39.48 = 0.5584 m.

items.q: A body of moment of inertia 0.1 kg m squared is suspended from a wire of torsional stiffness 2.5 N m per radian. Take pi as 3.142 and calculate the period of twist in s.
items.s: The period is twice pi times the square root of the moment of inertia divided by the torsional stiffness = 1.26 s.

items.q: A spring of constant 120 N/m is stretched by 0.15 m. Calculate the stored energy in J.
items.s: Stored energy is half the spring constant times the extension squared = 0.5 x 120 x 0.15 x 0.15 = 1.35 J.

items.q: An oscillator has a total energy of 0.4 J. Calculate its stored energy when its displacement is 0.75 of the amplitude.
items.s: Stored energy varies as the square of the displacement, so it is 0.4 x (0.75 x 0.75) = 0.225 J.

items.q: A lightly damped oscillator of initial amplitude 0.2 m decays with a damping coefficient of 1.5 per s. Calculate its amplitude after 1.5 s, in m.
items.s: The amplitude falls as the initial value times the exponential of minus the damping coefficient times the time = 0.0211 m.

items.q: The amplitude of a damped oscillator falls from 10 units to a steady value after 3 complete oscillations at the same fractional loss each time. Taking the amplitude after those oscillations as 10 units divided by the number of oscillations, calculate the amplitude after one oscillation in the same units.
items.s: Losing the same fraction each cycle divides the starting amplitude by the number of oscillations, giving 10 = 3.33 units.

items.q: A driven electrical oscillator has an inductance of 0.4 H and a capacitance of 50 microfarad. Taking pi as 3.142, calculate the frequency at which resonance occurs in Hz.
items.s: Resonance occurs at one divided by twice pi times the square root of inductance times capacitance = 35.58 Hz.

items.q: A wave of frequency 25 Hz travels with a wavelength of 1 m. Calculate its speed in m/s.
items.s: Wave speed is frequency times wavelength = 25 x 1 = 25 m/s.
items.t: Wave motion and the wave equation

items.q: A sound wave travels at 350 m/s with a wavelength of 0.25 m. Calculate its frequency in Hz.
items.s: Frequency is speed divided by wavelength = 350 / 0.25 = 1400 Hz.
items.t: Wave motion and the wave equation

items.q: A wave has a frequency of 10 Hz. Calculate its period in ms.
items.s: The period is the reciprocal of the frequency, 1/10 = 0.1 thousandths of a second, or 100 ms.
items.t: Wave motion and the wave equation

items.q: Two waves arriving at a point produce displacements of 4 units and 2 units in the same direction. Calculate the resultant displacement in the same units.
items.s: By superposition the displacements add directly when they act in the same direction, giving 4 + 2 = 6 units.

items.q: Two waves arriving at a point produce displacements of 6 units and 3 units in opposite directions. Calculate the magnitude of the resultant displacement in the same units.
items.s: Opposite displacements partly cancel, so the resultant magnitude is 6 - 3 = 3 units.

items.q: The fundamental frequency of a stretched string is 40 Hz. Calculate the frequency of its 4 harmonic in Hz.
items.s: The harmonics are whole number multiples of the fundamental, so the 4 harmonic is 40 x 4 = 160 Hz.

items.q: A string of length 0.5 m and mass per unit length 0.005 kg/m is stretched with a tension of 100 N. Calculate its fundamental frequency in Hz.
items.s: The wave speed is the square root of tension over mass per unit length, and the fundamental is that speed divided by twice the length = 141.4 Hz.

items.q: A string of length 0.75 m vibrates in 3 loops. Calculate the wavelength of the standing wave in m.
items.s: With 3 loops the wavelength is twice the length divided by the number of loops = 0.5 m.

items.q: A pipe closed at one end has a length of 0.2 m. Taking the speed of sound as 320 m/s, calculate its fundamental frequency in Hz.
items.s: A pipe stopped at one end has its lowest resonance at a quarter of a wavelength, so the frequency is 320 / (4 x 0.2) = 400 Hz.

items.q: A pipe open at both ends has a length of 0.2 m. Taking the speed of sound as 350 m/s, calculate its fundamental frequency in Hz.
items.s: A pipe open at both ends has its lowest resonance at half a wavelength, so the frequency is 350 / (2 x 0.2) = 875 Hz.

items.q: A resonance tube closed at one end resounds first at a length of 0.25 m. Neglecting the end correction, calculate the next resonant length in m.
items.s: Successive resonances in a stopped pipe are separated by half a wavelength, and the sequence goes from a quarter to three quarters of a wavelength, so the next length is 3 x 0.25 = 0.75 m.

items.q: A stopped resonance tube resounds at lengths of 0.18 m and 0.3 m. Calculate the end correction in m.
items.s: The end correction is half of (second length - three times the first length) = (0.3 - 3 x 0.18)/2 = -0.12 m.

items.q: A sound has an intensity 100000 times the threshold of hearing taken as 10^-12 W per m squared. Calculate its level in decibel.
items.s: The level is ten times the logarithm to base ten of the ratio to the threshold, giving 40 decibel.

items.q: A listener moves towards a stationary source of frequency 200 Hz at 20 m/s. Taking the speed of sound as 350 m/s, calculate the frequency heard in Hz.
items.s: A listener moving into the waves meets more of them each second, so the observed frequency is 200 x (350 + 20) / 350 = 211.4 Hz.

items.q: A source of frequency 250 Hz moves away from an observer at 25 m/s. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m/s, calculate the wavelength heard in m.
items.s: The waves are stretched, so the observed wavelength is (340 + 25) / 250 = 1.46 m.

items.q: An aircraft travels at 500 m/s in air where the speed of sound is 300 m/s. Calculate its Mach number.
items.s: The Mach number is the speed of the body divided by the speed of sound = 500 / 300 = 1.67.

items.q: Two waves of frequencies 320 Hz and 326 Hz travel together. Calculate the beat frequency heard in Hz.
items.s: The beat frequency is the difference of the two frequencies = 6 Hz.

items.q: Two waves of wavelength 0.6 m reach a point with a path difference of 0.25 of a wavelength. Taking pi as 3.142, calculate the phase difference in radian.
items.s: A path difference of 0.25 of a wavelength corresponds to the same fraction of a full cycle of 2 pi, giving 1.57 radian.

items.q: Two waves of wavelength 1.5 m differ in phase by 0.75 of a cycle. Calculate the path difference between them in m.
items.s: The path difference is the same fraction of a wavelength = 0.75 x 1.5 = 1.12 m.

items.q: A source has a coherence time of 5e-09 s. Taking the speed of light as 3.0 x 10^8 m/s, calculate its coherence length in m.

items.q: Two coupled pendulums of natural frequencies 5 Hz and 10 Hz swing together in step. Calculate the frequency of this common mode in Hz.

items.q: An oscillator has a total energy of 0.4 J. Calculate its stored energy when its displacement is 0.25 of the amplitude.
items.s: Stored energy varies as the square of the displacement, so it is 0.4 x (0.25 x 0.25) = 0.025 J.

items.q: A lightly damped oscillator of initial amplitude 0.8 m decays with a damping coefficient of 1 per s. Calculate its amplitude after 0.5 s, in m.
items.s: The amplitude falls as the initial value times the exponential of minus the damping coefficient times the time = 0.4852 m.

items.q: The fundamental frequency of a stretched string is 120 Hz. Calculate the frequency of its 3 harmonic in Hz.
items.s: The harmonics are whole number multiples of the fundamental, so the 3 harmonic is 120 x 3 = 360 Hz.

items.q: A listener moves towards a stationary source of frequency 800 Hz at 20 m/s. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m/s, calculate the frequency heard in Hz.
items.s: A listener moving into the waves meets more of them each second, so the observed frequency is 800 x (340 + 20) / 340 = 847.1 Hz.

items.q: A source of frequency 400 Hz moves away from an observer at 30 m/s. Taking the speed of sound as 360 m/s, calculate the wavelength heard in m.
items.s: The waves are stretched, so the observed wavelength is (360 + 30) / 400 = 0.975 m.

items.q: Two waves of wavelength 1.5 m differ in phase by 0.5 of a cycle. Calculate the path difference between them in m.
items.s: The path difference is the same fraction of a wavelength = 0.5 x 1.5 = 0.75 m.

items.q: Two coupled pendulums of natural frequencies 2 Hz and 8 Hz swing together in step. Calculate the frequency of this common mode in Hz.
items.s: In the in step mode the two swing as one system at the average of their separate frequencies = (2 + 8)/2 = 5 Hz.

items.q: An oscillator completes 2 cycles every second. Calculate its period in s.
items.s: The period is the reciprocal of the number of cycles per second = 1/2 = 0.5 s.

items.q: A body in simple harmonic motion has a maximum speed of 1.5 m/s at a rate of 3 rad/s. Calculate its amplitude in m.
items.s: Maximum speed is amplitude times angular frequency, so the amplitude is 1.5 / 3 = 0.5 m.

items.q: An oscillator of amplitude 0.2 m and angular frequency 5 rad/s starts from its greatest displacement. Calculate its displacement 0.2 s after release, in m.
items.s: The displacement is amplitude times the cosine of the angular frequency times the time = 0.2 x cos(1) = 0.1081 m.

items.q: A mass of 0.25 kg hangs on a spring of constant 160 N/m and oscillates. Take pi as 3.142 and calculate the period in s.
items.s: The period is twice pi times the square root of mass divided by spring constant = 0.2484 s.

items.q: A simple pendulum has an effective length of 0.4 m. Take g as 9.8 m/s squared and pi as 3.142, and calculate its period in s.
items.s: The period is twice pi times the square root of the length divided by g = 2 x 3.142 x sqrt(0.4/9.8) = 1.27 s.

items.q: A mass of 0.1 kg hung on a spring extends it by 0.05 m. Take g as 9.8 m/s squared and calculate the spring constant in N/m.
items.s: At rest the weight balances the restoring pull, so the constant is 0.1 x 9.8 / 0.05 = 19.6 N/m.

items.q: A body of moment of inertia 0.1 kg m squared is suspended from a wire of torsional stiffness 0.5 N m per radian. Take pi as 3.142 and calculate the period of twist in s.
items.s: The period is twice pi times the square root of the moment of inertia divided by the torsional stiffness = 2.81 s.

items.q: A spring of constant 40 N/m is stretched by 0.1 m. Calculate the stored energy in J.
items.s: Stored energy is half the spring constant times the extension squared = 0.5 x 40 x 0.1 x 0.1 = 0.2 J.

items.q: A mass of 0.5 kg oscillates with simple harmonic motion of amplitude 0.02 m at angular frequency 4 rad/s. Calculate the total energy of the oscillation in J.
items.s: Total energy is half the mass times the square of the angular frequency times the amplitude squared = 0.0016 J.

items.q: An oscillator transfers 0.5 J of energy in 0.5 s. Calculate the average rate at which energy is transferred in W.
items.s: The average rate is the energy divided by the time = 0.5 / 0.5 = 1 W.

items.q: Two tuning forks of frequencies 256 Hz and 261 Hz sound together. Calculate the number of beats heard per second.
items.s: The number of beats per second equals the difference of the two frequencies = 5 Hz.

items.q: The amplitude of a damped oscillator falls from 20 units to a steady value after 3 complete oscillations at the same fractional loss each time. Taking the amplitude after those oscillations as 20 units divided by the number of oscillations, calculate the amplitude after one oscillation in the same units.
items.s: Losing the same fraction each cycle divides the starting amplitude by the number of oscillations, giving 20 = 6.67 units.

items.q: A wave of frequency 50 Hz travels with a wavelength of 2 m. Calculate its speed in m/s.
items.s: Wave speed is frequency times wavelength = 50 x 2 = 100 m/s.
items.t: Wave motion and the wave equation

items.q: A sound wave travels at 320 m/s with a wavelength of 1 m. Calculate its frequency in Hz.
items.s: Frequency is speed divided by wavelength = 320 / 1 = 320 Hz.
items.t: Wave motion and the wave equation

items.q: A wave of frequency 500 Hz travels at 330 m/s. Calculate its wavelength in m.
items.s: Wavelength is speed divided by frequency = 330 / 500 = 0.66 m.
items.t: Wave motion and the wave equation

items.q: A wave has a frequency of 8 Hz. Calculate its period in ms.
items.s: The period is the reciprocal of the frequency, 1/8 = 0.125 thousandths of a second, or 125 ms.
items.t: Wave motion and the wave equation

items.q: A wave has a wavelength of 0.1 m. Calculate its wave number in per m.
items.s: The wave number is the reciprocal of the wavelength = 1/0.1 = 10 per m.

items.q: Two waves arriving at a point produce displacements of 3 units and 6 units in the same direction. Calculate the resultant displacement in the same units.
items.s: By superposition the displacements add directly when they act in the same direction, giving 3 + 6 = 9 units.

items.q: Two waves arriving at a point produce displacements of 6 units and 4 units in opposite directions. Calculate the magnitude of the resultant displacement in the same units.
items.s: Opposite displacements partly cancel, so the resultant magnitude is 6 - 4 = 2 units.

items.q: A standing wave has a wavelength of 0.5 m. Calculate the distance between two neighbouring nodes in m.
items.s: Neighbouring nodes are half a wavelength apart, so the distance is 0.5 / 2 = 0.25 m.

items.q: A string of length 0.8 m and mass per unit length 0.025 kg/m is stretched with a tension of 80 N. Calculate its fundamental frequency in Hz.
items.s: The wave speed is the square root of tension over mass per unit length, and the fundamental is that speed divided by twice the length = 35.36 Hz.

items.q: A pipe closed at one end has a length of 0.3 m. Taking the speed of sound as 320 m/s, calculate its fundamental frequency in Hz.
items.s: A pipe stopped at one end has its lowest resonance at a quarter of a wavelength, so the frequency is 320 / (4 x 0.3) = 266.7 Hz.

items.q: A pipe open at both ends has a length of 1 m. Taking the speed of sound as 360 m/s, calculate its fundamental frequency in Hz.
items.s: A pipe open at both ends has its lowest resonance at half a wavelength, so the frequency is 360 / (2 x 1) = 180 Hz.

items.q: A pipe closed at one end has a fundamental frequency of 80 Hz. Calculate the frequency of its 3 harmonic in Hz.
items.s: A stopped pipe supports only odd multiples of the fundamental, so the 3 harmonic is 80 x 3 = 240 Hz.

items.q: A stopped resonance tube resounds at lengths of 0.2 m and 0.3 m. Calculate the end correction in m.
items.s: The end correction is half of (second length - three times the first length) = (0.3 - 3 x 0.2)/2 = -0.15 m.

items.q: A source emits 0.2 W of sound energy that falls normally on a surface of area 2.5 m squared. Calculate the intensity at the surface in W per m squared.
items.s: Intensity is the energy crossing unit area per second = 0.2 / 2.5 = 0.08 W per m squared.

items.q: A source emitting 250 Hz approaches a stationary listener at 10 m/s. Taking the speed of sound as 320 m/s, calculate the frequency heard in Hz.
items.s: An approaching source crowds its waves, so the observed frequency is 250 x 320 / (320 - 10) = 258.1 Hz.

items.q: A source emitting 600 Hz recedes from a stationary listener at 10 m/s. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m/s, calculate the frequency heard in Hz.
items.s: A receding source stretches its waves, so the observed frequency is 600 x 340 / (340 + 10) = 582.9 Hz.

items.q: An aircraft travels at 1500 m/s in air where the speed of sound is 1500 m/s. Calculate its Mach number.
items.s: The Mach number is the speed of the body divided by the speed of sound = 1500 / 1500 = 1.

items.q: Two waves of frequencies 300 Hz and 305 Hz travel together. Calculate the beat frequency heard in Hz.
items.s: The beat frequency is the difference of the two frequencies = 5 Hz.

items.q: Two waves of frequencies 400 Hz and 404 Hz are superposed. Calculate the time from one loudness maximum to the next, in s.
items.s: Loudness maxima recur once per beat, and the beat frequency is 4 Hz, so the time between maxima is 1/4 = 0.25 s.

items.q: A simple pendulum has a period of 2.5 s. Take g as 9.8 m/s squared and pi as 3.142, and calculate its effective length in m.
items.s: The length is g times the square of the period divided by four pi squared = 9.8 x 2.5 x 2.5 / 39.48 = 1.55 m.

items.q: An oscillator has a total energy of 2 J. Calculate its stored energy when its displacement is 0.75 of the amplitude.

items.q: A lightly damped oscillator of initial amplitude 1 m decays with a damping coefficient of 0.5 per s. Calculate its amplitude after 3 s, in m.

items.q: The fundamental frequency of a stretched string is 150 Hz. Calculate the frequency of its 3 harmonic in Hz.

the constant total of moving and stored parts that a freely running oscillation keeps

items.s: energy budget of a swing: the constant total of moving and stored parts that a freely running oscillation keeps. The other options describe mean position, turning point, work done by a spring.

items.q: A body of moment of inertia 0.02 kg m squared is suspended from a wire of torsional stiffness 4 N m per radian. Take pi as 3.142 and calculate the period of twist in s.
items.s: The period is twice pi times the square root of the moment of inertia divided by the torsional stiffness = 0.4443 s.

items.q: The amplitude of a damped oscillator falls from 40 units to a steady value after 4 complete oscillations at the same fractional loss each time. Taking the amplitude after those oscillations as 40 units divided by the number of oscillations, calculate the amplitude after one oscillation in the same units.
items.s: Losing the same fraction each cycle divides the starting amplitude by the number of oscillations, giving 40 = 10 units.

items.q: A driven electrical oscillator has an inductance of 0.1 H and a capacitance of 25 microfarad. Taking pi as 3.142, calculate the frequency at which resonance occurs in Hz.
items.s: Resonance occurs at one divided by twice pi times the square root of inductance times capacitance = 100.6 Hz.

items.q: A string of length 1.2 m and mass per unit length 0.05 kg/m is stretched with a tension of 400 N. Calculate its fundamental frequency in Hz.
items.s: The wave speed is the square root of tension over mass per unit length, and the fundamental is that speed divided by twice the length = 37.27 Hz.

items.q: A stopped resonance tube resounds at lengths of 0.15 m and 0.36 m. Calculate the end correction in m.
items.s: The end correction is half of (second length - three times the first length) = (0.36 - 3 x 0.15)/2 = -0.045 m.

items.q: Two coupled oscillators of natural frequencies 4 Hz and 10 Hz exchange energy. Calculate the frequency of the slow transfer back and forth in Hz.
items.s: Energy passes across and back once per beat, so the transfer frequency is the difference of the two natural frequencies = 6 Hz.

items.q: A pendulum of small swing period 2 s is swung through an amplitude of 10 degrees. Using the correction that adds the square of the amplitude in degrees divided by 16000, calculate its period in s.
items.s: The period lengthens slightly with amplitude, giving 2 x (1 + 100/16000) = 2.01 s.

items.q: A body in simple harmonic motion has a maximum speed of 2.5 m/s at a rate of 6 rad/s. Calculate its amplitude in m.
items.s: Maximum speed is amplitude times angular frequency, so the amplitude is 2.5 / 6 = 0.4167 m.

items.q: A body oscillates with simple harmonic motion of amplitude 0.05 m at an angular frequency of 6 rad/s. Calculate its maximum acceleration in m/s squared.
items.s: Maximum acceleration is amplitude times the square of the angular frequency = 0.05 x 6 x 6 = 1.8 m/s squared.

items.q: A mass of 0.2 kg hangs on a spring of constant 40 N/m and oscillates. Take pi as 3.142 and calculate the period in s.
items.s: The period is twice pi times the square root of mass divided by spring constant = 0.4443 s.

items.q: A simple pendulum has an effective length of 0.25 m. Take g as 9.8 m/s squared and pi as 3.142, and calculate its period in s.
items.s: The period is twice pi times the square root of the length divided by g = 2 x 3.142 x sqrt(0.25/9.8) = 1 s.

items.q: A mass of 1.5 kg hung on a spring extends it by 0.02 m. Take g as 9.8 m/s squared and calculate the spring constant in N/m.
items.s: At rest the weight balances the restoring pull, so the constant is 1.5 x 9.8 / 0.02 = 735 N/m.

items.q: A spring of constant 40 N/m is stretched by 0.15 m. Calculate the stored energy in J.
items.s: Stored energy is half the spring constant times the extension squared = 0.5 x 40 x 0.15 x 0.15 = 0.45 J.

items.q: A mass of 0.1 kg oscillates with simple harmonic motion of amplitude 0.05 m at angular frequency 6 rad/s. Calculate the total energy of the oscillation in J.
items.s: Total energy is half the mass times the square of the angular frequency times the amplitude squared = 0.0045 J.

items.q: Two tuning forks of frequencies 500 Hz and 510 Hz sound together. Calculate the number of beats heard per second.
items.s: The number of beats per second equals the difference of the two frequencies = 10 Hz.

items.q: A lightly damped oscillator of initial amplitude 0.4 m decays with a damping coefficient of 1 per s. Calculate its amplitude after 1.5 s, in m.
items.s: The amplitude falls as the initial value times the exponential of minus the damping coefficient times the time = 0.0893 m.

items.q: A wave of frequency 40 Hz travels with a wavelength of 0.8 m. Calculate its speed in m/s.
items.s: Wave speed is frequency times wavelength = 40 x 0.8 = 32 m/s.
items.t: Wave motion and the wave equation

items.q: A sound wave travels at 360 m/s with a wavelength of 5 m. Calculate its frequency in Hz.
items.s: Frequency is speed divided by wavelength = 360 / 5 = 72 Hz.
items.t: Wave motion and the wave equation

items.q: A wave of frequency 400 Hz travels at 360 m/s. Calculate its wavelength in m.
items.s: Wavelength is speed divided by frequency = 360 / 400 = 0.9 m.
items.t: Wave motion and the wave equation

items.q: A wave has a wavelength of 4 m. Calculate its wave number in per m.
items.s: The wave number is the reciprocal of the wavelength = 1/4 = 0.25 per m.

items.q: Two waves arriving at a point produce displacements of 3 units and 2 units in the same direction. Calculate the resultant displacement in the same units.
items.s: By superposition the displacements add directly when they act in the same direction, giving 3 + 2 = 5 units.

items.q: The fundamental frequency of a stretched string is 150 Hz. Calculate the frequency of its 4 harmonic in Hz.
items.s: The harmonics are whole number multiples of the fundamental, so the 4 harmonic is 150 x 4 = 600 Hz.

items.q: A string of length 1.5 m vibrates in 4 loops. Calculate the wavelength of the standing wave in m.
items.s: With 4 loops the wavelength is twice the length divided by the number of loops = 0.75 m.

items.q: A pipe closed at one end has a length of 0.1 m. Taking the speed of sound as 350 m/s, calculate its fundamental frequency in Hz.
items.s: A pipe stopped at one end has its lowest resonance at a quarter of a wavelength, so the frequency is 350 / (4 x 0.1) = 875 Hz.

items.q: A pipe open at both ends has a length of 0.3 m. Taking the speed of sound as 360 m/s, calculate its fundamental frequency in Hz.
items.s: A pipe open at both ends has its lowest resonance at half a wavelength, so the frequency is 360 / (2 x 0.3) = 600 Hz.

items.q: A pipe closed at one end has a fundamental frequency of 80 Hz. Calculate the frequency of its 5 harmonic in Hz.
items.s: A stopped pipe supports only odd multiples of the fundamental, so the 5 harmonic is 80 x 5 = 400 Hz.

items.q: A resonance tube closed at one end resounds first at a length of 0.2 m. Neglecting the end correction, calculate the next resonant length in m.
items.s: Successive resonances in a stopped pipe are separated by half a wavelength, and the sequence goes from a quarter to three quarters of a wavelength, so the next length is 3 x 0.2 = 0.6 m.

items.q: A source emits 0.1 W of sound energy that falls normally on a surface of area 4 m squared. Calculate the intensity at the surface in W per m squared.
items.s: Intensity is the energy crossing unit area per second = 0.1 / 4 = 0.025 W per m squared.

items.q: A source emitting 250 Hz approaches a stationary listener at 10 m/s. Taking the speed of sound as 350 m/s, calculate the frequency heard in Hz.
items.s: An approaching source crowds its waves, so the observed frequency is 250 x 350 / (350 - 10) = 257.4 Hz.

items.q: A source emitting 800 Hz recedes from a stationary listener at 40 m/s. Taking the speed of sound as 360 m/s, calculate the frequency heard in Hz.
items.s: A receding source stretches its waves, so the observed frequency is 800 x 360 / (360 + 40) = 720 Hz.

items.q: A listener moves towards a stationary source of frequency 400 Hz at 10 m/s. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m/s, calculate the frequency heard in Hz.
items.s: A listener moving into the waves meets more of them each second, so the observed frequency is 400 x (340 + 10) / 340 = 411.8 Hz.

items.q: A source of frequency 800 Hz moves away from an observer at 25 m/s. Taking the speed of sound as 330 m/s, calculate the wavelength heard in m.
items.s: The waves are stretched, so the observed wavelength is (330 + 25) / 800 = 0.4437 m.

items.q: An aircraft travels at 1500 m/s in air where the speed of sound is 350 m/s. Calculate its Mach number.
items.s: The Mach number is the speed of the body divided by the speed of sound = 1500 / 350 = 4.29.

items.q: Two waves of frequencies 256 Hz and 258 Hz travel together. Calculate the beat frequency heard in Hz.
items.s: The beat frequency is the difference of the two frequencies = 2 Hz.

items.q: Two waves of frequencies 400 Hz and 410 Hz are superposed. Calculate the time from one loudness maximum to the next, in s.
items.s: Loudness maxima recur once per beat, and the beat frequency is 10 Hz, so the time between maxima is 1/10 = 0.1 s.

items.q: Two waves of wavelength 1.5 m differ in phase by 0.25 of a cycle. Calculate the path difference between them in m.
items.s: The path difference is the same fraction of a wavelength = 0.25 x 1.5 = 0.375 m.

items.q: Two coupled pendulums of natural frequencies 1 Hz and 6 Hz swing together in step. Calculate the frequency of this common mode in Hz.
items.s: In the in step mode the two swing as one system at the average of their separate frequencies = (1 + 6)/2 = 3.5 Hz.

items.q: An oscillator of amplitude 0.2 m and angular frequency 12 rad/s starts from its greatest displacement. Calculate its displacement 0.5 s after release, in m.
items.s: The displacement is amplitude times the cosine of the angular frequency times the time = 0.2 x cos(6) = 0.192 m.

items.q: A stopped resonance tube resounds at lengths of 0.2 m and 0.55 m. Calculate the end correction in m.

items.q: A source has a coherence time of 2e-08 s. Taking the speed of light as 3.0 x 10^8 m/s, calculate its coherence length in m.
items.s: Coherence length is the speed of light times the coherence time = 3.0 x 10^8 x 2e-08 = 6 m.

items.q: A pendulum of small swing period 2 s is swung through an amplitude of 25 degrees. Using the correction that adds the square of the amplitude in degrees divided by 16000, calculate its period in s.

items.q: A body oscillates with simple harmonic motion of amplitude 0.05 m at an angular frequency of 5 rad/s. Calculate its maximum acceleration in m/s squared.

items.q: A simple pendulum has an effective length of 2 m. Take g as 9.8 m/s squared and pi as 3.142, and calculate its period in s.

items.q: A mass of 5 kg hung on a spring extends it by 0.15 m. Take g as 9.8 m/s squared and calculate the spring constant in N/m.

items.q: A spring of constant 50 N/m is stretched by 0.02 m. Calculate the stored energy in J.

items.q: A mass of 2 kg oscillates with simple harmonic motion of amplitude 0.1 m at angular frequency 8 rad/s. Calculate the total energy of the oscillation in J.

items.q: An oscillator transfers 1 J of energy in 0.5 s. Calculate the average rate at which energy is transferred in W.
items.s: The average rate is the energy divided by the time = 1 / 0.5 = 2 W.

items.q: An oscillator has a total energy of 0.8 J. Calculate its stored energy when its displacement is 0.75 of the amplitude.
items.s: Stored energy varies as the square of the displacement, so it is 0.8 x (0.75 x 0.75) = 0.45 J.

behaviour in which the size of the restoring influence grows faster or slower than the displacement
driving an oscillator by changing one of its own properties rhythmically rather than by an outside push
the small swing simplification that treats the restoring influence of a hanging bob as proportional to its displacement

a tube stopped at one end, supporting only odd multiples of the lowest frequency
a region of a sound wave where the particles are spread apart

the number of loudness maxima heard per second from two nearly equal frequencies
the property of two waves that keep a fixed phase relation over time
the condition of two waves whose crests arrive at opposite instants
items.s: phase difference: the fraction of a cycle by which one wave leads or lags another. The other options describe coherence, beat frequency, out of phase.

superposition principle
node
fundamental

a moving emitter whose waves are stretched so the observed rate falls
the apparent change in the rate at which a source is heard because of relative motion

two or more oscillating bodies linked so that energy passes repeatedly between them
a vibrating body whose restoring influence is not proportional to the displacement
the lengthening of the period of a hanging oscillator that occurs as its swing grows

items.q: Select the statement that correctly explains coupled oscillators.

two or more oscillating bodies linked so that energy passes repeatedly between them
driving an oscillator by changing one of its own properties rhythmically rather than by an outside push

the number of loudness maxima heard per second from two nearly equal frequencies

the motion of an oscillator driven by a repeated external push

the resting place of an oscillator where no restoring pull acts
a small heavy bob hanging on a light thread from a fixed point
